   northwest Georgia early Monday morning.

   for rain on Thursday as a a system moves through the area.

 - Seasonal temperatures continue this week, with increasing
   confidence that the coldest temperatures of the season so far
   will arrive next weekend.

.SHORT TERM...
(Today through Tuesday)
Issued at 249 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Dry, benign weather conditions will persist through the short term 
period with surface high pressure centered to the west of the 
forecast area. Low temperatures this morning are expected to be 
between 32 and 36 degrees in portions of far north and west Georgia. 
Considering these temperatures and light winds, another Frost 
Advisory is in effect for these areas through 9 AM EST this morning. 
Lows will be in the low 40s elsewhere across the forecast area. High 
temperatures this afternoon will rise into the upper 60s to low 70s 
in north Georgia and mid 70s in central Georgia. A reinforcing shot 
of dry air will contribute to dewpoints in the upper 30s to low 40s 
today. RH values could briefly flirt with 25% for an hour or two in 
south-central Georgia this afternoon, though not for long enough to 
warrant a Fire Danger Statement considering remaining green 
vegetation.

A weak mid-level ridge will extend from the northern Gulf towards 
north Georgia by Tuesday morning, which will lead to a slight 
increase in temperatures throughout the day. Low temperatures 
tonight into early Tuesday are expected to be moderated to the upper 
30s to low 40s. A few locations in the highest elevations of far 
north Georgia may briefly drop into the mid 30s. Highs on Tuesday 
afternoon are expected to rise into the 70s areawide.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday night through Sunday)
Issued at 249 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Pleasant and dry weather continues through the middle of the week 
with high pressure parked over the region. Temperatures will warm up 
slightly, but remain around normal with highs in the 70s, and 
overnight lows in the upper 30s to low 40s. Confidence in the 
details of the forecast start to drop off for the second half of the 
week, but there is great model agreement on the overall pattern with 
a strong trough dropping over the Eastern US. This system will 
likely support at least slight rain chances for portions of North GA 
Thursday into Friday, before the associated cold front moves through 
and brings in a cool and dry airmass for next weekend. It is looking 
increasingly likely that this will be the coolest airmass of the 
season thus far, with lows at or below freezing across much of the 
area, and high temperatures topping out in the 50s to low 60s.

&&

Patchy fog will be possible in portions of east-central GA,
including MCN, until 13Z this morning. Otherwise, VFR

the day, diminishing to 3-6 kts by 02Z.

notable airmass differences behind the front should allow 
temperatures to still warm into the upper 50s to mid 60s on

precipitation chances is still anticipated mid to late week.

the associated surface low tracks, which will then factor into 
the location of greatest shower coverage. At this distance, 
locally higher chances exist near and south of I-80. While low 
to mid-level lapse rates this far north are not especially

elevated instability to produce a few lightning strikes or small
hail. Currently hold off on a formal mention in the gridded 
forecast, with the slightly better potential existing in central
Illinois.

rounding a closed upper low over Ontario as the broader upper 
trough descends across the eastern CONUS. One such vort may dive
across the area on Thursday, which could bring showers (and 
perhaps a few wet snowflakes) well inland. The resultant colder

temperatures would likely limit or even prevent snow 
accumulations. Nevertheless, it continues to look like snow will
likely mix in with the lake effect showers at times.

west of there until spring of 2027.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Much cooler conditions Thursday through Saturday, along with 
chances for precipitation. 

Model guidance is in very good agreement that a very deep trough 
will dig southward across the Eastern half of the CONUS late in the 
week. There continues to be pretty good agreement that a longwave 
pattern with troughing in the East and ridging in the West will set 
up within the Polar Jet stream, while the subtropical jet looks to 
also become active across the southeastern CONUS. The big point of 
contention is how exactly all of these features are going to 
interact with one another when it comes to impacts in our area.

we'll be in the warm advection ahead of a developing low. Highs are 
generally expected to be in the in the upper 50s and lower 60s. An 
area of low pressure is expected to form downstream of the digging 
trough, but there's still some spread with respect to where exactly 
it will form and how it will track. There is also the biggest 
question of if cold air will be in place ahead of this system, or 
will it lag behind. In mid-November, that can be very hard to 
achieve outside of the mountains, so that will be something to 
really keep an eye on as we get closer to this system occurring. 
Further east, right now the pattern seems to favor a rainy solution 
Thursday into Friday, and that is reflected in most of the recent 
model guidance and their respective ensembles.

At any rate, the upper low that will pivot over the region late
Friday and into this weekend and bring in a substantially 
cooler air mass in to the region. It is not out of the question 
to get some rain/snow showers further east into Saturday morning
under the upper low, but as of now, am not expecting any 
impactful accumulations. 

The Alleghenies will have the greatest chance for accumulating snow, 
but even there, there's still considerable spread, due to the

Issued at 200 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Weak mid level ridging in the Eastern Gulf will gradually move 
over the region today and into Tuesday. At the surface, high 
pressure centered off to the north will continue to slowly push 
eastward during this time frame. These two features will be the 
ones driving the weather pattern over South Florida through the 
early portion of the week. In general, rather light easterly winds
will prevail across most areas today and Tuesday. This easterly 
wind flow will aid in lower level moisture advection during this
time frame which will cause PWAT values to slowly and gradually 
rise across South Florida. While plenty of dry air will remain in
place across the mid levels, there will be just enough lower 
level moisture in place to support a low end chance of shower 
development each afternoon. Shower chances will be mainly driven 
by the development of the sea breezes each afternoon. Any showers 
that do develop will remain low topped, however, some of the 
stronger shower activity will have the potential to produce brief 
heavy downpours, especially over areas where sea breeze and other 
mesoscale boundary collisions take place. High temperatures today 
and Tuesday will rise into the lower to mid 80s across most areas,
however, upper 80s will be possible across portions of Southwest 
Florida each afternoon mainly along and south of Alligator Alley. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday night through Sunday)
Issued at 200 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Heading towards the middle of the week, the weak mid level ridging 
shifts into the western Atlantic as a mid level shortwave passes 
over the Southeast. While this shortwave will remain well off to the 
north, it will turn the mid level winds more southwesterly and will 
begin to draw in some deeper moisture over the region. At the 
surface, high pressure over the area will gradually begin to 
weaken as it pulls further into the western Atlantic. This will 
also cause a surface wind shift as well making the general 
synoptic wind flow light out of the south Southeast during this 
time frame. Since the shortwave will remain pretty far up to the 
north, the main forcing mechanism for shower development will be 
the sea breeze boundaries on Wednesday afternoon and evening. With
500mb heights lowering and some colder air moving in aloft, 
instability will gradually increase across the region which could 
allow for some thunderstorm development later on Wednesday 
afternoon into Wednesday evening. While chances for strong 
thunderstorm development will remain rather low, it cannot be 
entirely ruled out especially where mesoscale boundary collisions 
take place. The stronger thunderstorms could contain heavy 
downpours and gusty winds. High temperatures on Wednesday will 
generally rise into the lower to mid 80s across most areas, 
however, some upper 80s will be possible across portions of 
Southwest Florida. 

For the second half of the week, an amplifying mid level trough 
will rapidly push across the Eastern Seaboard on Thursday and will
remain parked in place heading into Friday. At the surface, 
developing low pressure will gradually move through the Mid 
Atlantic region and then off the Northeastern Coastline as the end
of the week progresses. The cold front associated with this 
system will extend southwestward and gradually approach and move 
through South Florida during the end of this week. As the cold 
front approaches, the pressure gradient will tighten causing winds
to increase out of the southwest on Thursday. While confidence is
increasing that this front will be on the stronger side, the 
latest global and ensemble guidance suite still remains in 
disagreement on the timing of the frontal passage across South 
Florida.

The ECMWF suite still shows a faster and more progressive solution 
bringing the front through Thursday night into early Friday morning. 
The GFS camps show a bit of slower solution, holding off the 
frontal passage till later Friday morning. This will have direct 
impacts on the sensible weather across the region especially 
heading into Friday. The ECMWF solutions would feature a quick 
moving front, with lower chances of showers and thunderstorms as 
the best dynamics race well off to the northeast. The GFS 
solutions would favor higher chances of showers and thunderstorms 
lingering later into Friday morning especially across southern
areas. The current forecast as it stands now increases the 
chances of showers and thunderstorms for Thursday into Friday 
morning. If trends start to favor the slower frontal passage 
solutions, showers and thunderstorms could linger into Friday 
afternoon as well across portions of the region. This will 
continue to be monitored as the week progresses. 

Behind the front, strong high pressure will build in from the north 
as winds rapidly shift and increase out of the west northwest 
heading into the upcoming weekend. This will allow for strong cold 
air advection to take place and bring in much drier air as well for 
Saturday and Sunday. Confidence continues to increase that this will 
be the coolest airmass of the fall season so far across South 
Florida and temperatures will be below normal through the upcoming 
weekend. This will continue to be monitored as the rest of the 
week progresses.

.SHORT TERM...
(Now through Thursday) 
Issued at 1105 PM CST Sun Nov 8 2026

Split upper flow continues this evening. A Northern stream shortwave 
trough was over the eastern Great Lakes and New England, followed by 
an upper ridge, then a second trough extending from Saskatchewan to 
off the Pacific Northwest coast. A southern stream trough was 
near El Paso. At the surface, high pressure extended from near 
Memphis to near Amarillo. The southern stream trough was pulling 
high level moisture from the Pacific northeastward into our area, 
with satellite imagery showing an extensive cirrus shield from the
Florida Panhandle westward across much of Texas and northern 
Mexico.

The 09/00z soundings here and at JAN show essentially no moisture 
below 700 mb, with mid and low level RH values below 20 percent. 
Late evening temperatures were mainly in the 50s, except on the
south shore of Lake Pontchartrain, where portions of New Orleans
metro area were in the mid 60s.

The northern stream shortwave track is currently far enough north to 
not have a large impact over the area for at least the next 36 hours.
The southern stream shortwave will eventually shear out to the 
east, transiting the local area Tuesday night and Wednesday 
morning. Expect quite a bit of mid and high level cloud cover with
this feature, but if any precipitation were to make it to the 
surface, it wouldn't amount to much. Currently a dry forecast. 

Once the southern stream shortwave gets out of the way, a rather 
strong northern stream shortwave will move through the upper and mid 
Mississippi River Valley toward the Atlantic Coast Wednesday night. 
The associated cold front will drive through the local area late 
Wednesday night and Thursday morning, and be offshore by midday. It 
wouldn't be an absolute surprise to see a very narrow band of 
showers on the leading edge of the front, but the most likely 
scenario is a dry frontal passage, with potentially rapid clearing 
behind the front. 

Cirrus clouds overnight likely will prevent temperatures from 
bottoming out as they did Sunday morning, with overnight lows 
remaining in the 40s and 50s in most areas. Those cirrus clouds may 
be the only thing that keeps high temperatures below 80 degrees in

northern Mid- Atlantic. The model guidance, including ensemble

.SHORT TERM...
Issued at 1145 PM PST Sun Nov 8 2026
(Tonight through Tuesday)

Dry weather continues over our forecast area due to a nearly 
stationary long wave ridge centered over the southwestern states. 
Cirrus clouds with the southern extent of the polar jet stream are
moving over the North Bay while to the south it is clear. Nocturnal
radiative cooling, most pronounced south of the cirrus clouds, is
allowing continental air to cool (higher pressure), setting up a 
light land breeze in contrast to the much of above Nov normal sea 
surface temps in the 60s as much as +10F to +11F above Nov normal 
(air in contact with the warmer sea surface temps equals lower 
pressure). Surface winds flow from high pressure to low pressure, 
which is keeping the warm maritime influence held to the coastline
or even nudged slightly offshore. Sea surface temps as warm as 
they are could easily keep coastal night-time/morning minimum 
temperature much warmer (e.g. San Francisco Aug 2015 set about a 
1/2 month of record high min temps, recall El Nino of 2015-2016), 
but remarkably at this time so far this has not been the case 
because of continental influence. November (vs August) brings 
occasional mid-latitude weather influences, much lower sun angle,
longer night time cooling hours.

Cooling tonight through daybreak Monday will produce additional 
low clouds and patches of fog. Because of the much above normal 
sea surface temperatures, water vapor availability is much more 
robust. Daytime sea breezes temporarily usher higher water vapor 
and hazy conditions inland, then when the winds turn neutral to a 
light land breeze, cooling is introduced (cooling described above)
and it is easy to reach saturation. Patchy dense fog may redevelop
tonight and Monday morning. Will monitor satellite and observations
and issue a dense fog advisory if needed.

Daytime highs Monday and Tuesday will continue slightly above 
normal with highs in the upper 60s at the coastline to the 70s and
lower 80s inland. Night-time lows will be in the 40s and 50s. A 
very weak 500 mb trough in the flow will pass by this time 
tomorrow night otherwise high pressure will prevail through early 
week.

(Tuesday night through next Sunday)

An increase in northern hemispheric long wave troughs is occurring
and will continue to hold during this time-frame. One long wave 
trough will strengthen over the northeastern Pacific and another 
long wave trough will strengthen downstream over the eastern 
states. In the 120 hour time-frame, out to Friday, the leading 
edge of strong polar jet stream winds will dig southward forming a
closed 500 mb low ~ 300-400 miles to our west-southwest Thursday.
Steering winds will continue to drive the newly formed closed 500
mb low toward southern California. This may leave a cold frontal 
passage with a chance of rain for our forecast area on Friday, 
though this is a low confidence forecast since model output is 
varying on rain amounts. Friday is five days out which is about 
the max we can rely on for global model output in the complex 
seasonal transition period of fall-winter. Dynamic strengthening 
is forecast upstream and downstream, both within the long wave 
trough over the east and to our west, but also with the ridge in 
between, nudged slightly forward during this time. If the upstream
long wave trough is able to slowly advance eastward, this should 
increase the chance of rain here, possibly to a greater chance

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 322 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Now through Tuesday Night...

Surface high pressure and northwesterly upper-level flow continue to 
prevail across the region this morning. With relatively calm winds 
and clear skies, decent radiational cooling will allow for daybreak 
conditions to be rather chilly. While it will not be as cold as 
yesterday, a Frost Advisory remains in effect until 10 AM EST for 
temperatures in the low to mid 30s. River valley fog is expected to 
develop over the next few hours, quickly dissipating after sunrise.

The persisting surface and upper air regimes will result in near 
normal temperatures and dry conditions. A return to widespread highs 
in the 60s comes this afternoon, continuing into Tuesday. There is 
the potential for some locations to reach 70 Tuesday afternoon, with 
the highest likelihood in west central Kentucky (40-60% chance per 
latest REFS). Overnight lows will still be on the colder side, 
ranging from the mid 30s to low 40s Monday and Tuesday night. 
Chances for frost will decrease after this morning, with the latest 
REFS, NBM, and LREF outputting less than 15% chances for 
temperatures below 35. 

By Tuesday afternoon, the upper-level pattern briefly shifts to more 
of a zonal regime. In addition, a weak shortwave will move eastward 
and skirt by just off to our south. Even if the wave did shift its 
trajectory northward, the limited moisture in place would prevent 
any appreciable precipitation from occurring over us.

Wednesday through Sunday...

The overall synoptic pattern begins to shift considerably by the 
middle portions of the work week. As a shortwave over the northern 
Plains swigs southeastward, the subtropical and polar jets will 
begin to interact and phase with each other. The combination of 
these features will result in cyclogenesis and the formation of a 
robust low pressure system over the eastern Great Lakes and Ohio 
Valley regions. 

Chances for precipitation will return by late Wednesday into 
Thursday as the cold front from the low begins to push through the 
area. The timing, placement, and progression of the shortwave and 
the phasing of the subtropical and polar jets will play an important 
role as to how much precipitation we get. Another factor in this 
will be the limited moisture return ahead of the system moving 
thorugh. While a narrow swath of PW values of 0.6-0.75" (~75th 
percentile climatologically) will help us get some accumulations, 
ensemble guidance is only outputting less than 0.5" through Friday 
across the area.

Once the cold front passes through, a cold airmass will fill in from 
behind, setting up a cool end to the work week, as well as the 
weekend. Afternoon highs on Thursday will be in the 50s, dropping to 
the mid to upper 40s Friday and Saturday. Temperatures Friday 
morning will be near or just above freezing, with a return to 
widespread below freezing temperatures Saturday and Sunday morning. 
If enough post-frontal moisture sticks around the area, there is the 
chance for some snow flurries late Thursday into Friday, especially 
along and east of the I-75 corridor. A few of the LREF members do 
pick up on light snowfall, so we will continue to see how things 
trend in the guidance as the week progresses. In addition to the 
cold air filling in behind the front, surface high pressure will 
build in overhead, resulting in dry conditions going into next 
weekend.

the Lower Mississippi River Valley to drive a southwest breeze
around 10 mph in the afternoon. Highs in the upper 50s to

.LONG TERM...
Issued 1025 PM CST Sun Nov 8 2026

Wednesday through Sunday:

On Wednesday, high pressure slides southeast into Manitoba and a 
deepening trough in the jet dives southeast from the Dakotas. Low
pressure develops over IA / IL in response to the trough 
Wednesday morning, with the trough and low tracking east into the
Ohio River Valley / eastern Great Lakes Wednesday night. QG ascent
from the approaching trough and developing low create 35-50% 
rain chances across the CWA Wednesday, with a developing north 
breeze and highs in the low 50s. 

As both pressure systems intensify and the low exits east, north
winds become gusty across Lake Michigan Wednesday night through
Friday, with Thursday featuring the strongest winds. Some 30-40 
mph wind gusts are looking likely across far eastern WI Thursday,
particularly along the Lake MI shoreline. 

Healthy lake effect convection tends to emerge with Lake Water
Temp to 850 mb temperature deltas over 13 Celsius; cold air 
arriving late this week could max out the temperature delta 
closer to 17 to 23 Celsius. With steady north winds down the long
axis of the lake from Wednesday night through Saturday, we expect
a north-south oriented single band of lake effect convection on
Lake MI, which could wobble east-west at times, occasionally 
making landfall on either side of the lake depending on the exact
wind direction. For counties bordering the lake in our CWA, this
will mean ~20-50% chances for precipitation at times from
Wednesday night through Friday, with chances generally < 10% into
Saturday as winds turn northwest. Rain is favored with the vast 
majority of these showers, though there will be periods of time
(mainly in the overnight and early morning hours) where some
snowflakes could mix in. I'll detail 2 specific timeframes below.

Late Wednesday night into early Thursday morning (inland temps in
the low/mid 30s, shoreline temps around 40) we could see a few 
snowflakes mix in with the rain if the precip were to travel far 
enough inland (west edge of shoreline counties, or the 2nd tier of
counties). And from Thursday evening into Friday morning (inland 
temps briefly reach the upper 20s, shoreline temps bottom out in 
the mid 30s) we could see some rain-snow mix or even pure 
snowfall at times. There's no guarantee (yet) that the lake effect
precip will make landfall during these specific timeframes, and 
outside of that it'll likely be all rain. Additionally, the 
figures I've provided for temperatures are the 2-meter air temps. 
Getting the land-surface or pavement temps to fall below freezing
could prove difficult with the accompanying lake-effect cloud
cover, and as such we are not currently forecasting 
accumulating snow. That said, trends in the temperature forecast
will be followed closely; things could change.

Winds turn northwest and decelerate into Saturday, pushing any
lingering lake effect precip away from WI. Dry weather expected
through the weekend, with highs rising from the 40s (Saturday) 
into the 50s (Sunday).

DISCUSSION...

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as 
the energetic jet stream resides mostly across Canada. Stacked low 
centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations. 

Brief but strong warm up on Saturday as strong ridging over the 
Plains advances eastward over the Great Lakes. ECMWF is a touch 
warmer (~18C at 850mb) than GFS (-16C) Saturday with strong 
southwesterly flow into the region. Current forecast is for temps to 
touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later. 

This warmup will be brief as attention the turns to TS Isaias which 
is set to make landfall over MS Friday evening then getting drawn 
northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

MARINE...

Moderate southwesterly winds gradually weaken this evening as a cold 
front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass, 
and given the rejuvenated low-level jet winds, mixing likely 
delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around

marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft

.FORECAST UPDATE...
Issued at 822 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Surface analysis this morning shows high pressure over Arkansas and 
TN, with a ridge axis extending north across IL, building east into 
Indiana. Aloft, water vapor shows a Pacific stream of moisture 
flowing across ID and MT to the upper midwest, running into a ridge 
axis, before diving southeast toward the middle Atlantic States. 
Subsidence was in place over MI and IN on the lee side of the ridge. 
GOES19 show clear skies over Indiana. Dew points were mainly in the 
middle and upper 30s.

Dry and mostly sunny weather is expected to continue this afternoon. 
Forecast soundings through the day show a dry column as Central 
Indiana will be protected as the upper ridge and surface high remain 
in control. Overall, ongoing forecast remains in good shape. Highs 
should reach lower to middle 60s.

&&

.DISCUSSION (Today through Sunday)...
Issued at 307 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

Today through Tuesday night...

Quiet weather conditions are expected to persist as upper ridging 
and surface high pressure build eastward into the region. Current 
satellite and surface observations depict surface high pressure 
centered near the central CONUS with clear skies across Indiana. A 
very weak pressure gradient is contributing to light or even calm 
winds at times early this morning. These light winds combined with 
clear skies could allow for patchy fog to develop in 
climatologically favored locations towards daybreak. Any fog that 
develops should quickly mix out after sunrise.   

Model guidance depicts a shortwave moving across the Great Lakes 
Region around Tuesday morning with an associated weak cold front 
pushing into central Indiana. No precipitation is expected from the 
approaching boundary due to gulf moisture remaining cutoff. The weak 
frontal boundary could cool temperatures slightly. 

Return flow will moderate temperatures through Tuesday before the 
cold front arrives. Look for highs to generally range from the low 
to mid 60s with lows in the upper 30s to low 40s. Highs on Tuesday 
could end up being a few degrees cooler than currently forecasted 
depending on when the front arrives. A quicker FROPA Tuesday morning 
would likely limit daytime heating. 

Wednesday through early next week... 

A deepening shortwave trough moving in from the northwest on 
Wednesday is expected to promote surface cyclogenesis across the 
Midwest. Latest ensemble guidance depicts the surface low developing 
near Illinois and continuing to strengthen as it progresses 
eastward. Increasing dynamics from these features combined with 
sufficient gulf moisture surging northward supports increasing rain 
chances. Scattered to numerous showers are possible and weak 
destabilization late Wednesday may support a few thunderstorms. 

The parent trough is expected to continue deepening across the 
eastern CONUS through late this week with strong cold air advection 
across central Indiana. Broad cyclonic flow, steepening lapse rates, 
and lingering low-level moisture will continue to promote the 
potential for showers on Thursday. Latest guidance continues to 
suggest precipitation will linger through Friday given a favorable 
fetch off of Lake Michigan. Isolated rain/snow showers are possible 
to end the work week, but QPF amounts are expected to be minimal due 
to very limited moisture and weak forcing.

The aforementioned low pressure system and parent trough will shift 
eastward over the weekend while an amplified upper ridge builds into 
the central CONUS. Warm air advection ahead of the upper ridge is 
expected to help moderate temperatures over the weekend into early 
next week. Drier conditions are also likely. Look for a 
roller coaster in temperatures from the middle of this week 
through early next week. Highs in the low to mid 60s Wednesday 
will quickly cool down well into the 40s by Friday before then 
warming back up into the 50s on Sunday.

year. Expect overnight lows to remain in the upper 30s (eastern

The aforementioned upper low to our southwest will continue
sliding eastward on Tuesday, however guidance keeps this system
south of our area, with no impacts expected. Highs on Tuesday

associated cold front pushing through. There's still model

however a drier airmass looks to dominate for much of the
area as the frontal boundary pushes through, keeping things 
mostly dry. The exception lies in the east/northeast portion of 
the CWA, where better forcing and moisture exists, resulting in

The timing of the frontal passage will play a large role in

cold front.

Behind this system, cooler air will filter in, dropping
temperatures a few degrees below normal in the 50s on Thursday,
and the upper 40s to low 50s on Friday. The overnights will be
chilly, with many locations dropping below freezing in the mid
20s to mid 30s Thursday and Friday nights.

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH TUESDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 206 AM CST Mon Nov 9 2026

The Mid-Mississippi River Valley will be positioned beneath west-
northwesterly upper-level flow through Tuesday. A shortwave trough 
within this flow will shunt the low-level ridge currently in place 
eastward and force a weak cold front into the CWA tonight that 
stalls thereafter. Weak forcing and limited moisture return will 
preclude precipitation and even much in the way of cloud cover from 
forming along the front. Accompanying these dry conditions, 
southwesterly to westerly low-level flow and weak WAA will support 
well-above average temperatures through Tuesday, including highs in 
the mid-60s to low-70s F. Radiational cooling is expected to be 
relatively efficient again tonight with a loose surface pressure 
gradient near the front and little cloud cover. These conditions 
could promote additional patchy river valley fog, but slightly 
warmer temperatures will be less favorable for contributions 
from steam fog formation processes.

&&

.LONG TERM /WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 206 AM CST Mon Nov 9 2026

A potent Alberta Clipper including an amplifying upper-level 
shortwave trough will traverse the Mid-Mississippi River Valley on 
Wednesday, facilitating the passage of a cold front through the CWA 
trailing a deepening surface cyclone across the Midwest. As is 
commonly the case with Alberta Clippers, the majority of associated 
precipitation will be to the north of the surface cyclone's track 
and north of the CWA, but 40 to 60 percent of ensemble model 
membership has scattered showers developing along/east of the 
Mississippi River as moisture and forcing increase along the cold 
front. There are still some timing differences, however, that will 
influence how far west these showers develop. Steepening lapse rates 
with mid-level cooling may sufficiently compensate for modest 
moisture return to enable a few thunderstorms to develop as 
deterministic model guidance projects a narrow corridor of 500 to 
1000 J/kg of MUCAPE. Additionally, a tightening surface pressure 
gradient will result in occasional wind gusts of 20 to 28 kt on 
Wednesday.

Behind the cold front and initial shortwave trough, longwave 
troughing will amplify across the eastern CONUS with deep cyclonic 
flow ensuing over the Mid-Mississippi River Valley. As multiple 
additional shortwave troughs and/or vorticity maxima rotate around 
the parent longwave trough, the pattern appears favorable for 
periodic light showers or drizzle through Friday. With uncertain 
timing of each feature and a common dry bias in longer-rage model 
guidance in these patterns, the forecast is currently dry after 
Wednesday. Strong and persistent low-level CAA and increased cloud 
cover will at least result in coldest temperatures we have seen so 
far this season including highs in the 40s to low 50s F and lows in 
the mid-20s to mid-30s F. Confidence is high in Friday being the 
coldest day of the period with high temperatures falling to warm out 
of the 40s F, followed by a nearby surface anticyclone favoring 
widespread low temperatures in the 20s F if clouds clear enough.

Next weekend, global model guidance agrees that mid-level heights 
will begin rising and the anticyclone will shift to the east of the 
region as downstream longwave troughing progresses eastward. This 
pattern change will lead to a warming trend but there are 
significant disparities on how quickly this process takes place, 
which determine how quickly temperatures will warm. Accordingly, the 
NBM interquartile temperature range inflates to 15 F by next Sunday, 
although even the 25th percentile still demonstrates an underlying 
warming trend.
